nameStory: The Ultronia Underwing gets its name from the spectacular hidden surprise beneath its wings - while the forewings are camouflaged in mottled browns and grays, the hindwings flash brilliant dark red bands when the moth takes flight. The scientific name 'ultronia' means 'of one's own accord' in Latin, perhaps referring to how this moth willingly reveals its stunning underwings when disturbed, creating a startling display that can confuse predators.
description: The Ultronia Underwing is a medium-sized moth that's a master of disguise by day and a showstopper by night. When resting on tree bark with wings folded, it looks like just another piece of mottled bark, but when it flies, it reveals striking dark red and black banded hindwings that flash like warning signals. These moths have a wingspan of about 2-2.5 inches across, making them substantial enough to notice when they're attracted to your porch light. They're part of a fascinating group called underwing moths, all famous for their hidden colorful hindwings.

idTips.label: Hidden red underwings
idTips.description: The most spectacular feature - dark red hindwings with black bands that are only visible when the moth spreads its wings or flies, creating a sudden flash of color against the night

idTips.label: Bark-like forewings
idTips.description: Mottled gray-brown forewings with intricate patterns that feel papery to the touch and perfectly mimic tree bark when the moth rests during the day

idTips.label: Substantial size
idTips.description: A hefty moth with a wingspan nearly as wide as your palm, noticeably larger than most moths you'll see at lights, with a robust, fuzzy body

idTips.label: August flight time
idTips.description: Active in late summer when most other large moths have finished their season, making them stand out at porch lights during warm August evenings

idTips.label: Daytime hiding behavior
idTips.description: Rests head-down on tree trunks during the day, pressed flat against bark with wings folded like a tent, nearly impossible to spot until you're inches away

habitat: Look for Ultronia Underwings in mixed deciduous forests and woodland edges where their caterpillar food plants grow - especially areas with wild cherry trees, poplars, ash trees, and basswoods. They're also found in orchards and suburban areas with mature fruit trees like apples. The adults are strongly attracted to artificial lights, so check around porch lights, street lamps, and moth sheets in wooded neighborhoods during late summer.

seasonality.spring: No adult moths visible - eggs are hatching and tiny caterpillars are beginning to feed on newly emerging tree leaves.
seasonality.summer: Caterpillars are growing throughout early summer on host trees, but remain well-camouflaged and rarely seen. Adult moths begin emerging in late July.
seasonality.fall: Peak flight time in August when adults are most active and commonly seen at lights. Mated females lay eggs on tree bark before the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died and eggs overwinter on tree bark, waiting for spring warmth to hatch into the next generation of caterpillars.

funFact: When threatened, the Ultronia Underwing performs a magic trick worthy of a stage illusionist - it suddenly flashes its bright red underwings while making erratic flight movements, then just as quickly snaps them shut and seemingly vanishes against tree bark, leaving confused predators wondering where their colorful target disappeared to in the blink of an eye.
confusionNotes: The Ultronia Underwing is easily confused with its close relative, the Ilia Underwing, which has nearly identical bark-like forewings but sports bright orange-red (rather than dark red) hindwings. Memory trick: 'Ultronia = Ultra-dark red' while Ilia has the brighter, more orange-tinted red underwings.
contextualKnowledge: The underwing moths as a group were once considered some of the most challenging moths for collectors and scientists to identify, leading to many naming confusions in old field guides. Many species in this genus look nearly identical when resting, and their true identities are only revealed when they take flight and show their colorful hindwings.
compareHints: Compared to the Ilia Underwing, the Ultronia has distinctly darker, more wine-red hindwings rather than the bright orange-red of its cousin. While both species have similar bark-mimicking forewings and identical resting poses, the Ultronia's underwings lack the bright, almost flame-orange quality of the Ilia. The Ultronia also tends to be slightly more common in areas with wild cherry trees, while Ilia prefers oak-dominated forests.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Ultronia Underwing, the Ilia has that diagnostic white circle on the forewing that Ultronia lacks.
